On the last day of the laundromat, my father washed a single sock. He paid six dollars to do it. When I pointed out that he could have washed it in the sink, he said, “I could have washed it in the sink in 1987, too.”

That was the year he bought the place. The sock wasn’t from 1987. I checked.

I’d come with a recorder borrowed from the library. The idea was to get him talking about the laundromat: how he’d bought it with money from selling his taxi, how my mother had put a bowl of oranges by the change machine and gotten annoyed when people took them. I wanted to ask about the flood. I wanted to ask whether he remembered making me do my homework on top of dryer nine, which ran a little hotter than the others and kept my legs warm through my jeans.

He remembered the flood.

“Water came in,” he said.

I waited.

“From outside.”

I stopped the recorder.

At eleven, Mrs. Alvarez came in with her comforter. Dad had taken the sign down the night before, and she wanted to know why he’d done that if he was still open.

“Because I had a ladder yesterday,” he said.

“You could put up a paper sign.”

“I could.”

She stood there a moment, deciding whether the matter called for further intervention. Then she put her comforter in the big machine. Dad went over and opened the soap drawer for her, though she’d been coming in every Thursday since I was nine and knew how it worked.

He’d told me he was ready to be done. The new owner was going to sell tiles. There would be a rack of tiles you could pull out and tilt under a light, and a desk where you could sit down and discuss the cost of having a floor. Dad had shown me the plans. He was pleased that they’d decided to keep the little bathroom in the back.

Around noon I turned the recorder on again and left it on the folding table. I didn’t tell anybody. I wasn’t trying to catch a confession. I’d just noticed that as soon as I held it up, my father said everything twice as clearly and half as well.

A boy fed quarters into the change machine. It was an excellent machine, in that respect: it took a quarter and gave you a quarter. He kept doing it until his mother noticed.

The door made its familiar high noise. Dad had oiled the hinge any number of times. The noise turned out to come from the rubber sweep at the bottom, which he could have trimmed in thirty seconds. By the time he figured that out, he’d grown to like knowing when someone came in.

At two, Mrs. Alvarez folded her comforter with his help. For the first fold they stood far apart, arms spread. At each subsequent fold they stepped closer, until finally he pulled his hands out and she had the whole thing against her chest.

“What’re you going to do on Thursdays?” she asked him.

“I have to see about a tooth.”

“Every Thursday?”

“I don’t know how bad it is yet.”

She laughed, and then she asked him, quite seriously, to let her know.

The sock was still in the washer. I asked if he was going to dry it.

“No,” he said. “It’s yours.”

It was gray with a green heel. I’d bought a pack of them in college. He said he’d found it behind the lost-property bin when he pulled the bin out to sweep. I put it in my coat pocket. For the next hour, whenever I leaned against the folding table, I could feel the wet coming through.

We stayed until six, though nobody came in after four. Dad emptied the coin boxes, and I counted the quarters into paper sleeves. He kept sliding little piles toward me after I thought I’d finished. In the end we had one quarter that wouldn’t make up a roll. He went to the door and wedged it into the loose strike plate, which had rattled since the tile man came to measure.

That night, in my apartment, I listened to the recording. There was more of me on it than I’d expected. Me asking where the tape was. Me tearing it with my teeth. Me saying, “Dad,” three times, with no particular urgency, while I waited for him to turn around.

Then, in a stretch I didn’t remember at all, my father began to sing. It wasn’t loud enough to make out the words. I kept backing up, thinking I recognized the tune, and then losing it when a dryer came on.

I took the recorder over to his house the next morning. He was at the kitchen table eating toast on a paper towel. I played him the part with the singing and asked what song it was.

“That’s not me,” he said.

We listened again.

“It’s you.”

It was. I’d been standing by the folding table, putting tape on a box. With the dryer going I’d apparently felt free to sing.

“Your mother used to sing that,” he said.

I waited for him to name the song, but he didn’t know it either. He put another slice of bread in the toaster. While we waited for it to come up, I played the little stretch again, this time with the recorder between us on the table. There was a scrape I took for the box being dragged across the table. Then the dryer cut out, and you could hear my father, very close to the microphone, humming the next few notes. By then I’d stopped singing. He went on by himself for a little while.
